scenes.visual: Title card 'The Climbing Line' over a cartoon mountain in profile with horizontal temperature bands. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: GOLD line = the isotherm (or, in film 2, the food peak), the climate the species needs; GREEN band = the species (or its breeding); RED bracket = the gap between them; ORANGE tint = warming. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Mountains, beetles, birds and forests are simple cartoons; anything not computed is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: A mountain warms by zero point three degrees Celsius each decade. How far uphill must the beetles' range shift, to stay as cool as before?
scenes.caption: A mountain warms by 0.3 °C each decade. How far uphill must the beetles' range shift, to stay as cool as before?
scenes.visual: A small cluster of green beetle cartoons sits partway up the slope. On-screen: 'warming: 0.3 °C per decade'. A question mark floats above the slope with an up arrow.
scenes.narration: A mountain warms by 0.3 °C each decade. How far uphill must the beetles' range shift, to stay as cool as before?

scenes.tts: Picture the slope as stacked bands of temperature, warm at the bottom and cool at the top. The gold line is an isotherm, a line of equal temperature.
scenes.visual: Horizontal bands shade from warm (bottom) to cool (top). One GOLD horizontal line glows across the slope, labelled 'isotherm: a line of equal temperature'. A GREEN band, the beetle population, sits just above it, labelled 'species'.
scenes.narration: Picture the slope as stacked bands of temperature, warm at the bottom and cool at the top. The gold line is an isotherm, a line of equal temperature.

scenes.tts: This beetle lives only where it is cool enough. So the gold line marks the lower edge of its range, the warm edge.
scenes.visual: The GREEN band's bottom edge aligns exactly with the GOLD line; the slope below turns a faint ORANGE with a label 'too warm'. Label at the edge: 'range edge set by temperature'.
scenes.narration: This beetle lives only where it is cool enough. So the gold line marks the lower edge of its range, the warm edge.

scenes.tts: Now warm the whole mountain. Every band slides upward, and the gold line climbs with them. The beetle's climate is on the move.
scenes.visual: An ORANGE tint creeps up the slope over a decade counter (0 to 1). All bands slide up; the GOLD line climbs smoothly. The GREEN band stays put for now, leaving a sliver of space below the gold line.
scenes.narration: Now warm the whole mountain. Every band slides upward, and the gold line climbs with them. The beetle's climate is on the move.

scenes.tts: How fast does the line climb? That depends on how quickly air cools with height, a slope's lapse rate. Here it cools zero point six degrees every hundred metres.
scenes.caption: How fast does the line climb? That depends on how quickly air cools with height, a slope's lapse rate. Here it cools 0.6 °C every 100 metres.
scenes.visual: A vertical ruler appears at the mountain's side with ticks every 100 m; beside each tick a thermometer drops by one step. Label: 'lapse rate: 0.6 °C per 100 m'.
scenes.narration: How fast does the line climb? That depends on how quickly air cools with height, a slope's lapse rate. Here it cools 0.6 °C every 100 metres.

scenes.tts: Divide the warming rate by the lapse rate. The result is the climate velocity, the speed of the isotherm. On this slope, it is fifty metres uphill each decade.
scenes.visual: On-screen sum builds piece by piece: '0.3 °C per decade ÷ 0.6 °C per 100 m = 0.5 × 100 m = 50 m per decade'. The GOLD line climbs exactly 50 m on the ruler as the decade counter ticks to 1. Label: 'climate velocity'.
scenes.narration: Divide the warming rate by the lapse rate. The result is the climate velocity, the speed of the isotherm. On this slope, it is fifty metres uphill each decade.

scenes.tts: Now let the population move, as beetles settle higher and low ones die out. The green band climbs, but slower than the gold line.
scenes.visual: Decade counter runs 1 to 3. The GREEN band creeps upward at a slower, unlabelled rate (labelled 'schematic').
scenes.narration: Now let the population move, as beetles settle higher and low ones die out. The green band climbs, but slower than the gold line.

scenes.tts: The red bracket between band and line is the gap. Each decade the line pulls further ahead. If the beetles started in step, the gap is the difference in speeds, times the time.
scenes.visual: A RED bracket between the top of the GOLD line's climb and the GREEN band's lower edge grows with each decade tick. On-screen: 'gap = (isotherm speed − species speed) × time', with a footnote 'if the species started in step'.
scenes.narration: The red bracket between band and line is the gap. Each decade the line pulls further ahead. If the beetles started in step, the gap is the difference in speeds, times the time.

scenes.tts: So moving is not the same as keeping up. A range keeps up only by moving as fast as its isotherm.
scenes.visual: The GREEN band gets a tag 'moving'; the RED bracket gets a tag 'not keeping up'. Banner: 'measure the gap (temperature-set range)'.
scenes.narration: So moving is not the same as keeping up. A range keeps up only by moving as fast as its isotherm.

scenes.tts: Now set a flat plain beside it. There, temperature changes toward the pole, and far more slowly with distance.
scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: the mountain. Right: a flat map strip running from warm (south, ORANGE) to cool (north), with a GOLD isotherm crossing it as a vertical line. A distance scale in kilometres along the bottom.
scenes.narration: Now set a flat plain beside it. There, temperature changes toward the pole, and far more slowly with distance.

scenes.tts: So on the flat, how far toward the pole gives the same cooling as one metre uphill? A metre, a hundred metres, or about a kilometre?
scenes.visual: Left: a 1 m step on the mountain glows. Right: three option tags hover over the plain: '1 m', '100 m', '~1 km'.
scenes.narration: So on the flat, how far toward the pole gives the same cooling as one metre uphill? A metre, a hundred metres, or about a kilometre?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame; a 5-second countdown; caption 'Predict: how far poleward equals 1 m uphill?'.

scenes.tts: In one European example, about a kilometre and a half. A short climb buys the cooling of a long journey. The exchange rate varies by place.
scenes.visual: The '~1 km' tag lights up; a GOLD bar 1 m tall on the mountain is linked by a dotted line to a GOLD bar about 1.5 km long on the plain. Label: 'same cooling: 1 m up ≈ 1.5 km poleward (one European example; varies by region and season)'.
scenes.narration: In one European example, about a kilometre and a half. A short climb buys the cooling of a long journey. The exchange rate varies by place.

scenes.tts: So raw distances cannot say which shift kept up. Each shift is judged against its own isotherm, on its own slope or plain.
scenes.visual: Each side gets its own RED gap bracket: mountain band against mountain line, plain band against plain line. A crossed-out arrow between '17 km' and '11 m' labelled 'raw distances: not comparable'.
scenes.narration: So raw distances cannot say which shift kept up. Each shift is judged against its own isotherm, on its own slope or plain.

scenes.tts: A twenty eleven synthesis pooled many studies of land species. The median shifts were about seventeen kilometres poleward and eleven metres uphill each decade.
scenes.caption: A 2011 synthesis pooled many studies of land species. The median shifts were about 17 kilometres poleward and 11 metres uphill each decade.
scenes.visual: Two counters: 'median poleward: 16.9 km per decade', 'median uphill: 11.0 m per decade', source line 'Chen and colleagues, Science, 2011'.
scenes.narration: A 2011 synthesis pooled many studies of land species. The median shifts were about 17 kilometres poleward and 11 metres uphill each decade.

scenes.tts: But the medians hide wide variation. Some species ran ahead of their isotherm, and many lagged behind it.
scenes.visual: Around each GOLD line, scattered GREEN dots appear (labelled 'schematic'), spread widely. On the plain, dots fall on both sides, centred near the line; on the mountain, more fall below it than above. The median marks as a small white tick among them.
scenes.narration: But the medians hide wide variation. Some species ran ahead of their isotherm, and many lagged behind it.

scenes.tts: One last warning. For a forest beetle, clearing the lower slope can lift the range's bottom edge, whatever the temperature does. A shift shows change, not its cause.
scenes.visual: On the mountain, the lowest strip of trees turns to bare brown fields; the GREEN band, labelled 'a forest beetle', has its bottom edge lift. A label: 'forest loss can also push a range uphill'. Banner: 'a shift shows change, not cause'.
scenes.narration: One last warning. For a forest beetle, clearing the lower slope can lift the range's bottom edge, whatever the temperature does. A shift shows change, not its cause.

scenes.tts: A range keeps up only by moving as fast as its isotherm.
scenes.visual: The full mountain: GOLD line climbing, GREEN band behind, RED bracket between. The words 'as fast as its isotherm' highlight in GOLD.
scenes.narration: A range keeps up only by moving as fast as its isotherm.

scenes.visual: Hex end card. Take-home line: 'A range keeps up only by moving as fast as its isotherm.'
